name: Bohtan Neo-Aramaic
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Fox, Samuel Ethan. 2007. The Story of Mem u Zine in the Neo-Aramaic Dialect of Bohtan. In Cynthia L. Miller (ed.), Studies in Semitic and Afroasiatic Linguistics Presented to Gene B. Gragg (SAOC 60), 69-80. Chicago: Oriental Institute. Open PDF:https://isac.…
catalog_quote: There is a strong penultimate stress,3 and stress moves when a suffix is added: arxe ‘mill’ arxota ‘mills’ kebœn ‘I (masculine) want’ kebœnna ‘I (masculine) want her’ abra ‘son’ abreni ‘our son’ In most dialects, adding a clitic to a word generally does not cause stress to shift, as in this Jilu example: múdi ‘what’ múdi-la ‘what is it (feminine)?’ However, in Bohtan, even when clitics are added the stress usually shifts: brota ‘daughter, girl’ brotá-se ‘also the girl’ bata ‘house’ batá-la ‘she is (in) the house’ In the verb paradigm, stress sometimes deviates from the usual strong penultimate pattern. ... [fn. 3:] Because the great majority of words have penultimate stress, stress is not marked unless it is not penultimate.

new_statements.quote: Talking a look at the stress one can say that in the C.B dialect words are mostly stressed on the penultimate, e.g. báxta “woman”. [...] There are, of course, some exceptions as the suffix wa/wo, that denotes the past, never takes the stress as for example *patƏx+wa>potawa “he would open”, or the L‐set suffixes (that are used in order to mark the subject and the object on the Preterite verbs) are not stressed. [...] in the dialect of Bohtan if the enclitic copula is added as a consequence the stress changes its position from the penultimate syllable of the independent word to the penultimate syllable of the composite word, as it is shown in the example batá‐na.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Per the item actually at the listed URL (a 2015 Leiden student paper by Giordana Pagano summarising Fox 2002/2007/2009, not Fox 2002 itself): Christian Bohtan words are 'mostly' stressed on the penultimate syllable (báxta); the stress domain includes the enclitic copula, so stress shifts to the penult of word+copula (batá-na); the past suffix -wa/-wo and the L-set subject/object suffixes on preterite verbs never take stress; a few lexical items are non-penultimate (Ənsṓn 'human being', áġdode 'each other').
new_statements.exceptions: Past marker -wa/-wo never stressed (*patƏx+wa > potawa); L-set suffixes on preterite verbs unstressed; lexical exceptions Ənsṓn 'human being' (final) and áġdode 'each other' (initial/antepenult); independent pronouns penultimate except 1pl/2pl; enclitic copula counts inside the stress unit (batá-na), unlike Jilu.
new_statements.identity_note: Pagano's paper describes the Christian dialect of Bohtan ('C.B') as documented by Fox from the Gardabani (Georgia) / Krymsk-Novopavlovsk (Russia) diaspora speakers originally from Ruma, Šwata and Borb; this is the same variety as Glottolog boht1238 'Gardabani Bohtan Neo-Aramaic' and as the catalog's Fox 2007 source. Contrasts drawn in the paper with Jilu, Hertevin, Jewish Arbel and Trans-Zab dialects (final stress in nominals) are about other NENA varieties, not Bohtan.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote confirmed verbatim in the open publisher PDF we hold/text of Fox 2007 at p. 70 + fn. 3. (2) The deciding source is a first-hand sketch by the dialect's sole documenter, publisher-text grade, 2007; the classification (penultimate word stress, stress shifting with suffixes and usually with enclitics, listed verb-paradigm exceptions) is exactly what the passage says. (3) It is not the best available description: Fox's 2009 Gorgias reference grammar (175 pp, Glottolog 'grammar') exists and is not yet obtained; it is paywalled (DOI 10.31826/9781463217327) and only a copy whose provenance we do not cite copies appear online, so nothing was downloaded. No instrumental or dedicated prosody study of Bohtan was found.
